content: Emergency Medical Technician-Intermediate (EMT-I) is a mid-level prehospital emergency medical provider in the United States. EMT-Is are not designed to provide definitive medical care but are trained to enhance prehospital critical care and deliver rapid on-scene treatment. They typically work in ambulances alongside EMT-Basics and EMT-Paramedics. EMT-Is are authorized to perform more advanced medical interventions than EMT-Basics and are often trained to provide advanced life support. EMT-I/85 The EMT-I/85 certification allows for several invasive procedures beyond the basic level. These include intravenous (IV) therapy, the use of multi-lumen airway devices, and, in some states, endotracheal intubation. EMT-I/85 providers are generally permitted to administer the same medications as EMT-Basics, such as oxygen, oral glucose, activated charcoal, epinephrine auto-injectors (Epi-Pens), nitroglycerin, and metered-dose inhalers (MDIs). In many states, they are also allowed to administer 5% and 50% dextrose in water (D5W and D50, respectively). Medication protocols vary by state. For instance, in New Hampshire, EMT-Is can administer additional medications such as Narcan (naloxone), atropine, thiamine, and nebulized albuterol. EMT-I/99 The EMT-I/99 certification is the highest level of EMT-Intermediate training and is closest to the paramedic level. EMT-I/99 providers are trained to perform advanced procedures such as needle decompression for tension pneumothorax, endotracheal intubation, nasogastric tube insertion, use of cardiac event monitors and electrocardiograms (ECGs), and administration of medications to manage specific cardiac arrhythmias. State-Specific Variations and Higher Levels of EMTs Some states have additional or alternative levels of EMT certification beyond the national standards established by the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT). For example: Alaska: EMT-II certification is similar to the EMT-I/85 standard, while EMT-III is closer to the EMT-I/99 level. EMT-IIIs can perform additional procedures, such as wound suturing, if trained and authorized by a sponsoring physician. California: The EMT-I designation refers to the national EMT-Basic level and should not be confused with EMT-Intermediate. Iowa: EMT-Basics can administer Epi-Pens, insert Combi-Tubes, and maintain non-medicated IVs. EMT-Intermediates can establish IVs and perform all EMT-Basic skills. Iowa Paramedics are equivalent to NREMT-Intermediate/99, while Paramedic Specialists are equivalent to NREMT-Paramedics. Iowa also offers a Critical Care endorsement for Paramedic Specialists. Michigan: EMT-I/85 is referred to as EMT-Specialist, but this level is being phased out as EMT-Basic standards approach the paramedic level. New York: The state offers an Advanced EMT-Critical Care (AEMT-CC) certification, which is similar to the national EMT-I/99 standard. New York also has an AEMT-Intermediate certification equivalent to EMT-I/85. However, New York City does not recognize advanced EMT certifications; providers are either EMT-Basics or paramedics. Oklahoma: Previously recognized an EMT-Cardiac level, which has been phased out. Providers at this level were either upgraded to paramedics or downgraded to EMT-I. Rhode Island: EMT-Cardiac is the first level of advanced life support (ALS) and falls between EMT-I and EMT-P. EMT-Cardiac providers can administer more cardiac medications than EMT-Is but fewer than paramedics. This certification is commonly required by fire departments in the state. Tennessee: EMT-IVs are trained to the NREMT-Basic standard with additional training in advanced airway management, IV therapy, and administration of medications such as epinephrine, albuterol, D50W, glucagon, nitroglycerin, and aspirin. The state is considering transitioning to an EMT-B, EMT-Advanced, and EMT-P format. Vermont: EMT-I '03 certification is unique to the state and falls between EMT-I/85 and EMT-I/99. EMT-I '03 providers can administer medications such as albuterol, aspirin, D50, epinephrine, glucagon, naloxone, nitroglycerin, and thiamine, in addition to EMT-Basic medications. Virginia: EMT-Enhanced is the first level of ALS and allows providers to perform procedures such as IV therapy, endotracheal intubation, chest decompression, and administration of medications like D50, glucagon, albuterol, epinephrine, and, in some cases, narcotics. The state has phased out its Cardiac Tech program. Wisconsin: EMT-IV Technicians are EMT-Basics with additional training to start IV lines, treat hypovolemic shock, and administer medications such as Narcan and D5. This certification is often used in rural areas where hospitals are sparse, and advanced life support (ALS) may take longer to arrive. Each state has unique protocols and certifications tailored to its specific needs, often influenced by geography, population density, and available medical resources.
